claims.not_understood: The meanings of the three parts - identity, action, cycle - have never been tested; only their positions have. The program cannot yet say which signs are animal signs or sky signs from its own data (that needs a visual classification crosswalk it does not have), so the companion claims about animal openings and sky-sign endings are untested or only structurally supported. A three-part pattern is also weaker evidence than it may look: many record-keeping systems, linguistic or not, develop fixed field orders. What would change the picture: a visual classification of the sign classes, so the semantic version of the claim can be tested instead of the positional shadow of it.

explanation_record.explanation_text: The program tested the shape of this claim, and the shape held up. In the test recorded on the claim (the positional test in the program's analysis files), 805 of 2,267 inscriptions of three or more signs followed the opening-middle-ending structure - 35.5 percent, against 0.6 percent expected by chance, a lift of about 59 times. The test also found the position-strong signs the pattern needs: 40 signs that strongly prefer the opening, 20 that strongly prefer the ending, and 61 for the middle. That is why the status is partially supported. The limit of the support is written in the test's own verdict, and it should be quoted rather than softened: the pattern is 'consistent with both Hunt model and Dravidian suffix model. Cannot distinguish between them without visual sign classification.' In other words, the check shows a three-part positional pattern exists. It does not show that the parts carry the meanings Hunt assigns them, and the same pattern is equally consistent with a rival account in which the closing signs are simply word endings in a language.

audit_note_2026_10_22.note: Prior-art note (spec-025 material audit, 2026-10-22): a three-part positional structure for Indus texts is published prior art - Wells 2015, ch. 3 (pp. 24-25): 'Patterned texts consist of three fields (Initial, Medial and Terminal)' (FULL TEXT); behind it Sinha et al. 2010 (arXiv:1005.4997, FULL TEXT), Yadav 2009, and Fuls's seven positional classes (explicitly syntactic, not semantic), with roots in Mahadevan 1977 and Kondratov 1976. What the Hunt document adds is semantic labels on that structure, not the structure itself.

spec071_retirement_append_2026_10_25.closing_state: RETIRED - the sky-signs endings question is untestable in this programme
spec071_retirement_append_2026_10_25.closing_finding: The celestial class is empty in every classification this programme can honestly build. Asset A v1 (187 rows) and Asset A v2 (552 rows), both built from published sources only, entered blind, the second on the repaired keying surface that keys 556 of the 557 signs the documented corpus uses, each contain zero sky_cycle rows - because no ruled published source depicts any keyed sign as a sky object. The verbatim labels beneath the kind column were checked for this closure: across 552 rows, the only celestial words in any published label describe ray or sunburst features of other depicted objects, in three rows, none an identification of a sign as a celestial body (each excluded in advance by Spec 071 section 4.1). A class cannot be tested at a floor of 30 occurrences when it has no members. The claim stands UNTESTED, and the question is retired in this programme - not falsified, not supported: untestable here, because the published-identification layer the programme's discipline requires does not contain the class the question is about. The empty celestial class is the line's closing finding.
